card.name: Merengue tipico
card.era: Oldest style of merengue; dates to the 1840s-1850s
card.tagline: The oldest, accordion-led Cibao style of merengue.
card.profile: Merengue tipico (also merengue cibaeno, colloquially perico ripiao) is the oldest surviving style of merengue, originating in the rural Cibao around Santiago in the mid-19th century. Early ensembles used strings, but two-row diatonic button accordions replaced them when Germans arrived in the 1880s via the tobacco trade, joined by guira, tambora and (historically) the marimba box bass, later electric bass, saxophone and congas. It is fast (2/4), with rhythms including merengue derecho and pambiche, and a climactic improvisational jaleo/mambo section - the 'country music' of the DR (English Wikipedia; Smithsonian Folkways).
card.insight: Per ethnomusicologist Sydney Hutchinson and Smithsonian Folkways, a strong transnational merengue tipico scene has connected Santiago and New York City since the 1960s, reshaping the tradition while keeping it alive in the diaspora.
